title: Background services and graceful shutdown
summary: BackgroundService, what an unhandled exception does to the host, how shutdown reaches your loop, and a queue-backed worker that survives a bad job.

steps.title: BackgroundService: a loop the host owns
body: A hosted service runs next to your endpoints for the life of the app. `BackgroundService` is the usual base class:
```csharp fragment
class OutboxPublisher(IServiceScopeFactory scopes, ILogger<OutboxPublisher> log) : BackgroundService
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))
using var scope = scopes.CreateScope();          // hosted services are singletons: make a scope for DbContext
await scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<Publisher>().PublishPendingAsync(stoppingToken);
// builder.Services.AddHostedService<OutboxPublisher>();
Facts that bite:
- Since **.NET 6**, an exception that escapes `ExecuteAsync` **stops the whole host** (`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost`).
Catch and log per item inside the loop; let only truly fatal errors escape.
- Since **.NET 10**, all of `ExecuteAsync` runs in the background, including the code before its first `await` (before, that part
ran during startup and could delay it). Code that must finish before the app serves traffic belongs in `StartAsync` of an
`IHostedService`, or in an `IHostedLifecycleService` hook.
- Hosted services are **singletons**. Never inject a scoped service (a `DbContext`) directly; create a scope per unit of work.

steps.prompt: A `BackgroundService` reads jobs from a channel. One job has a malformed payload and `JsonSerializer.Deserialize` throws inside `ExecuteAsync`, uncaught. What happens on .NET 8 or later with default settings?
options: The exception is logged and the host shuts down: the whole app stops, endpoints included
The bad job is skipped and the loop continues
The service restarts itself after a delay
Nothing is logged; the worker silently stops while the app keeps running
steps.explain: The last option was the behaviour before .NET 6, which was worse (a dead worker nobody notices). Today the default is to stop the host, so that the orchestrator restarts it and you notice. Either way: catch per item.

steps.title: Graceful shutdown, end to end
body: Kubernetes (or `docker stop`, or a Windows service stop) sends **SIGTERM**. Then:
1. The host triggers `IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping`; Kestrel stops accepting new connections.
2. Each hosted service's `StopAsync` runs: for a `BackgroundService` it **cancels `stoppingToken`** and waits for `ExecuteAsync` to end.
3. The host waits at most **`HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout`** (30 seconds by default since .NET 6). After that it stops waiting and
the process exits, whatever is still running.
4. Kubernetes waits `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (30 s by default) after SIGTERM, then sends **SIGKILL**.
So: keep `ShutdownTimeout` below the grace period; make `ExecuteAsync` stop **taking new work** when `stoppingToken` fires, but
decide deliberately whether to **finish the job in hand** (usually yes, if it is short) or abandon it (then it must be safe to retry,
for example because the message was not acknowledged).
```csharp fragment
builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(o => o.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(20));

steps.prompt: Put the shutdown of a pod in order.
lines: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to the container
`ApplicationStopping` fires and Kestrel stops accepting connections
The worker finishes its current job and leaves its loop
The host finishes stopping within `ShutdownTimeout` and the process exits
If anything is still running when the grace period ends, Kubernetes sends SIGKILL

steps.prompt: In a `BackgroundService` that processes queue messages: good practice or a bug?
items: `try { await HandleAsync(msg, ct); } catch (Exception e) when (e is not OperationCanceledException) { log.LogError(e, ...); }` per message
Injecting `AppDbContext` into the constructor of the hosted service
Creating a scope per message with `IServiceScopeFactory`
`ShutdownTimeout` of 60 s with Kubernetes' default 30 s grace period
Leaving the loop when `stoppingToken` is cancelled, after finishing the current message

steps.title: A job queue that survives a bad job
prompt: The API accepts jobs and a background worker runs them. Today one bad job takes the whole app down.
Keep the endpoints and fix the worker:
- `POST /jobs` with `{ "payload": "..." }` puts the payload on the bounded channel and answers **202 Accepted**;
- `JobWorker` runs each job; a job whose payload is `"boom"` throws. A failing job must be **counted as failed and logged**, and the
worker must **keep going**. Count with `Interlocked` (the worker and the endpoint run on different threads).
**Run checks** starts your app, posts `a`, `boom`, `b`, `c` and polls the stats.
starter: app.MapPost("/jobs", async (JobRequest req, Channel<string> queue, CancellationToken ct) =>
app.MapGet("/jobs/stats", (JobStats s) => new { done = s.Done, failed = s.Failed });
class JobStats { public int Done; public int Failed; }
class JobWorker(Channel<string> queue, JobStats stats) : BackgroundService
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
solution: app.MapPost("/jobs", async (JobRequest req, Channel<string> queue, CancellationToken ct) =>
app.MapGet("/jobs/stats", (JobStats s) => new { done = Volatile.Read(ref s.Done), failed = Volatile.Read(ref s.Failed) });
class JobStats { public int Done; public int Failed; }
class JobWorker(Channel<string> queue, JobStats stats, ILogger<JobWorker> log) : BackgroundService
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
catch (Exception e) when (e is not OperationCanceledException)
template: public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
var r = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/jobs", new { payload = "a" });
await Dojo.TryAsync("The app keeps serving after a bad job", async () =>
foreach (var p in new[] { "boom", "b", "c" }) await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/jobs", new { payload = p });
Dojo.Eq("The worker ran the three good jobs", "3", done);
Dojo.Eq("The bad job was counted as failed", "1", failed);
hints: Wrap the body of the `await foreach` in try/catch, so one job's exception does not leave `ExecuteAsync`.
`catch (Exception e) when (e is not OperationCanceledException) { Interlocked.Increment(ref stats.Failed); log.LogError(e, "Job {Payload} failed", payload); }`, and inject `ILogger<JobWorker> log`.
explain: The `when (e is not OperationCanceledException)` filter lets shutdown end the loop normally instead of counting it as a failed job.
In a real system the failed payload would also go to a dead-letter store so someone can look at it.
